subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The C-Price: Coffee's Benchmark
description: A quick win: understand The C-Price: Coffee's Benchmark.

hook.text: The 'C-price' is the global benchmark for Arabica coffee, set by traders on the New York commodity exchange.

buildup.text: It fluctuates based on supply, demand, weather, and speculation. Farmers must sell at or near this price.

discovery.text: When the C-price drops below $1 per pound, most farmers can't cover production costs—they lose money on every bag.

twist.text: Wall Street traders who've never touched a coffee bean influence pricing more than the farmers who grow it.

climax.text: Price volatility is coffee's central economic problem. Good years are followed by devastating crashes.

punchline.text: One number on a screen controls millions of farming lives.

quiz.question: What is the 'C-price' in coffee?
options: The global benchmark price for Arabica on commodity exchanges

details.summary: The C price is the benchmark commodity price for arabica coffee on the New York Intercontinental Exchange. It sets the floor for most global coffee transactions. When the C price drops below production costs, millions of farmers face financial ruin even as consumers see little change.
details.whyItMatters: The C price disconnects farm-level costs from market value. It is the single most powerful force driving poverty and prosperity in coffee-growing regions.
takeaways: The C price is the global benchmark for arabica coffee
It is traded on the New York Intercontinental Exchange
Low C prices can push farmers below production costs

faq.question: What determines the C price for coffee?
faq.answer: Supply and demand, weather forecasts, currency fluctuations, and speculative trading all influence it. A frost in Brazil or drought in Vietnam can spike prices overnight. The C price reflects market sentiment as much as actual supply conditions.

faq.question: Why does the C price matter so much to farmers?
faq.answer: Most coffee is bought and sold with the C price as the baseline. When it falls below production costs, which vary from 1 to 1.50 dollars per pound for many smallholders, farmers cannot cover expenses. Fair trade and direct trade attempt to decouple from this volatility.
